adjacent: Climate change contributes to food insecurity, so interventions which reduce climate change may improve equitable access to food.
Reducing climate change could prevent attraction of invasive species that favour a warmer climate.
Actions to reduce climate change by reducing carbon dioxide emissions will also reduce ocean acidification.
Reducing climate change will create fewer climate refugees, leaving more global citizens to live in peace and safety.
Climate change contributes to food insecurity, so interventions which reduce climate change may improve equitable access to food.
climate_change.description: Glasgow has no net contribution to global greenhouse gas emissions.
climate_change.target: Sectors most responsible for global warming are decarbonised and Glasgow has minimised the emissions embedded in its supply chains. Glasgow is not fed by industrial farming methods, especially for livestock with high Greenhouse Gas emissions, such as cows. Consumption levels of the heaviest emitters are curtailed, and specific sites responsible for very high emissions are targeted e.g. Glasgow Airport. Glaswegians eat primarily plant-based diets that create fewer Greenhouse Gases. Buildings are retrofit to Net Zero standards such as Passivhaus, to reduce our energy demand.

adjacent: Reducing air pollution will have positive impact on species abundance and biodiversity.
Reducing air pollution will have positive impact on species abundance and biodiversity.
air_pollution.description: Glasgow supports and requires activity in the city and its supply chains to eliminate contributions to global air pollution.
air_pollution.target: Public and active transport is enabled throughout the city, with lots of connected walking and cycling routes. Highly polluting forms of transport (including air travel) are minimised. Policy and financial support is available for initiatives such as Liveable Neighbourhoods and Low Emission Zones, to disincentivise car use and promote active travel and more widespread use of public transport. Glasgow reduces its industrial emissions footprint by ending the production and consumption of single-use or short-life items (including products imported from around the world).

adjacent: Reducing chemical pollution may create jobs in industries such as recycling/waste management, but may put other industries at risk, e.g. fast fashion retail.

More circular practices that reduce pollution could lead to reduced labour demand in supply chains that feed traditional linear economy models i.e. production of goods that are imported, consumed, discarded.
chemical_pollution.description: Glasgow is committed to minimising its material footprint. Glasgow has a Circular Economy that maximises re-use of resources, minimises its use of harmful chemicals across sectors and supply chains, and is a global leader in the remediation of polluted urban environments.
chemical_pollution.target: Glasgow's overall consumption is reduced, and the dominant consumerist culture is challenged by re-using, recycling, and repairing initiatives. Consumption of raw materials is minimised. Procurement policies and practices outlaw singleuse products, pollutants, and items designed for obsolescence. Urban design and waste management is improved to prevent pollutants from entering the biosphere e.g. Sustainable Urban Drainage Systems (SuDS) protect the water system from microplastics. Glasgow's procurement, construction, and waste management policies and procedures are transformed. Support is provided for alternative business models to keep materials and products circulating locally.

ocean_acidification.description: Glasgow contributes to protecting global oceans by having no net contribution to greenhouse gas emissions.
ocean_acidification.target: The sectors emitting most CO2 in Glasgow in 2022 - heating and transport - are fully decarbonised. Demand for CO2 burning activities is reduced overall, through investment in active and public transport, insulation and retrofit of buildings, and green local energy networks. Carbon Capture Storage is utilised on Vacant and Derelict Land sites.

biodiversity_loss.description: Glasgow uses its political influence and convening power to facilitate awareness raising, evidence generation and debate around biodiversity solutions.
biodiversity_loss.target: Glasgow carefully disincentivises supply chains and consumption practices that have negative consequences for global biodiversity, whether that is through pesticide use, CO2 emissions or waste management. Agriculture and fishing are less intensive, maintaining sustainable level of fish populations e.g. wild salmon. More urban allotments are used for food growing, leaving untouched land intact. Glaswegians understand the importance of biodiversity for human and planetary health through education and communication initiatives.

adjacent: Reducing nutrient runoff from excessive fertiliser use will improve food security, including supply chains that feed Glasgow.
Reducing nutrient runoff from excessive fertilizer use will make cycling water more feasible without needing to contend with algal blooms etc.
Reducing nutrient runoff from excessive fertilizer use will improve biodiversity, e.g. by reducing algal blooms and species loss etc.
Reducing nutrient runoff from excessive fertilizer use will improve biodiversity, e.g. by reducing algal blooms and species loss etc.
Reducing nutrient runoff from excessive fertiliser use will improve food stability by creating more diverse and sustainable food chains.
excessive_fertilizer_use.description: Farming practices in Glasgow's global supply chains are effective in minimising reliance on excessive fertilizer use. Glasgow supports and requires sustainable land use throughout its supply chains.
excessive_fertilizer_use.target: Glasgow's surrounding farmlands utilise permaculture or regenerative agriculture methods. We support small-scale, local, food businesses (both growing and selling). Glasgow does not waste food. We use any food excess for compost to enrich local soil health. Subsidy or tax relief is provided to sustainable or regenerative food businesses. We can use previously vacant and derelict sites for growing food, cycling water and regenerating soil, in order to reduce dangerous nutrient loading elsewhere e.g. further upstream Glasgow's rivers.

fresh_water_withdrawal.description: Glasgow contributes to a sustainable and fair global water footprint.
fresh_water_withdrawal.target: The water footprint of Glasgow's production and consumption is minimised. People in Glasgow adopt circular economy principles in their water consumption patterns. Supply chains are fed by sustainable practices in the food and textile industries. People eat predominantly plant-based diets, that are less water intensive than the production of meat. People in Glasgow have access to transparent, easy to understand information about how sustainable our overall use of water is, and the water footprint of our products. Communication campaigns inform residents about Glasgow's water footprint, and the volume of water required for everyday items (clothes, food etc.)

adjacent: Limiting land conversion may reduce the availability of land for construction of new and affordable housing.
Reduced land conversion will lead to better protection and conservation of biodiverse habitats.
Reduced land conversion will lead to better protection and conservation of biodiverse habitats.
Deforestation and land conversion can lead to outbreaks of pathogens, so protecting land and preserving biodiversity will increase disease resilience.
land_conversion.description: Glasgow's supply chain is built upon transparent and sustainable land use practices, ensuring responsible and accountable land management. Glasgow maximises its global influence to support restorative land use practices.
land_conversion.target: Glasgow makes use of urban allotments, vertical farming, and city rooftops, to reduce the amount of land used for agriculture, and allow more natural biodiversity to flourish. Food produced by industrial agriculture methods that cause deforestation is not imported into the city. Policy interventions incentivise good practice, penalise damage to natural landscapes, and empower communities to be involved in sustainable land management.

ozone_layer_depletion.description: Glasgow avoids using ozone-depleting chemicals and gases, and contributes to the development of alternatives through research and development.
ozone_layer_depletion.target: Raising awareness and education about the harms of ozone layer depletion, and which substances contribute to this. Support provided for suitable alternatives, and more ozonefriendly practices, such as more sustainable forms of transport in the city, strengthened by environmental regulation.

adjacent: Reducing air pollution through increased urban greening, active travel infrastructure and low emission zones could improve health (e.g. respiratory and cardiovascular).
Initiatives to reduce air pollution through increased active travel and cleaner public transport options could increase options for mobility.
Green and blue urban infrastructure intended to reduce air pollution will also help store carbon.
Green and blue urban infrastructure intended to reduce air pollution will also enhance wellbeing.
Green and blue urban infrastructure intended to reduce air pollution will also help regulate the temperature.
Reducing air pollution could also improve conditions for species abundance and protect biodiversity.
Reducing air pollution could also improve conditions for species abundance and protect biodiversity.
Local reductions in air pollution will contribute to global reductions in atmospheric pollutants.
Green and blue urban infrastructure intended to reduce air pollution will also help reduce climate change.
cleanse_the_air.description: All Glasgow citizens breathe healthy and unpolluted air, and pollutants are well below maximum statutory guidelines for health.
cleanse_the_air.target: Glasgow implements active travel infrastructure, Low Emission Zones, and urban greenery in public, private, and commercial spaces to minimize emissions from construction, transport, and industry. It uses policy levers to support the widespread capture of pollutants, both at individual and industrial levels.

adjacent: Rewilding and replanting initiatives that increase biodiversity could support sustainable job creation to develop and maintain these areas, positively impacting income and work, as well as attracting tourists to Glasgow to support job creation in this sector.

Initiatives that increase biodiversity through improved blue and green space will have a positive impact on health through benefits to mental health and providing space for physical activity. However, there is potential for negative health effects if new species or wildlife habitats bring parasites or more opportunities for disease spread. Increased allergens are possible from some plant life.
Rewilding and replanting initiatives that increase biodiversity, such as local species reintroduction, could provide opportunities for community benefit through inclusive participation.
Rewilding and replanting initiatives that increase biodiversity, such as local species reintroduction, could involve local schools and youth groups and can provide important education opportunities.
More biodiversity supports pollinators and worms, which are essential for food security.
Biodiversity protection work could inform the design of new housing sites so they can support greater local biodiversity.
Increased biodiversity of plants can store carbon.
Increased biodiversity of plants can cleanse the air.
Initiatives that increase biodiversity through improved blue and green space can enhance wellbeing, by providing spaces for leisure and opportunities for social connection.
Increased biodiversity of plants can help to regulate the temperature.
Increased biodiversity of plants can support efficient cycling of water and reduce flood risks.
More biodiversity supports pollinators and worms, which can contribute to building and protecting soil health, and stabilising/binding soil through habitat restoration can prevent soil erosion.
Increasing biodiversity locally has the potential to reverse damage to global wildlife populations.
Increased biodiversity of plants can reduce air pollution.
Stabilising and binding soil through habitat restoration to increase biodiversity can prevent nutrient runoff from excessive fertilizer use.
house_biodiversity.description: Glasgow and its surroundings have abundant and diverse local populations of native species.
house_biodiversity.target: Biodiversity protection and restoration are properly resourced and integrated into all planning priorities. Glasgow protects crucial pollinators and worms, creates well-connected habitats and wildlife corridors, and manages city parks and waterways to support wildlife habitats. It provides training opportunities for citizens of all ages to improve skills in managing green spaces for biodiversity and encourages rewilding and the planting of wildflower meadows.

adjacent: Green jobs could be created through large-scale decarbonisation and carbon capture and storage infrastructure, boosting income and work.
Regenerating vacant and derelict land for carbon storage could harness positive health co-benefits by removing toxins and heavy metals from the ground.
Remediating vacant and derelict land for carbon storage can help improve social equity, as sites are usually in deprived areas.
Regenerating vacant and derelict land for carbon storage could transform these sites into places for community activity and connection.
Using carbon capture and storage technology to create building materials can support housing activity.
Urban greening and other methods to store carbon will also remove other pollutants, helping to cleanse the air.
Increasing urban greening, and regenerating vacant and derelict land for carbon storage could transform these sites into places for recreation to enhance wellbeing.
Increasing urban greening to store carbon can also regulate the temperature.
Carbon capture and storage removes contaminants that might otherwise enter the water system and will improve the quality of water.
Carbon capture and storage solutions can help to protect soil by removing toxins
Remediation of vacant and derelict land for carbon capture may risk existing biodiversity in these unique habitats, but could also provide enabling conditions for alternative species.
Reducing atmospheric carbon emissions will reduce contributions to ocean acidification.
Reducing atmospheric carbon emissions will reduce contributions to climate change.
Using vacant and derelict land for carbon capture and storage will enable re-purposing of this land and reduce the need for further land conversion for human purposes.
Waste management as part of carbon storage solutions could reduce chemical pollution.
store_carbon.description: Glasgow stores more carbon in its trees, soils, greenspaces, and waterways than it releases. It maintains and protects its natural carbon sinks.
store_carbon.target: Glasgow focuses on decarbonizing the heating, transport, and construction sectors through the use of Nature-Based Solutions, net-zero construction materials, and repurposing industrial infrastructure for carbon sequestration. It supports the restoration of carbon sinks across the wider region, such as peatlands and seagrass.

adjacent: Sustainable drainage design will reduce the energy required for surface water pumping and waste water pumping and treatment.
Proper treatment of potentially contaminated water prior to reuse can have positive health impacts (e.g. reduce bacterial illnesses).
Rainwater harvesting can reduce mains water usage and therefore improve water security.
Costs of installing new equipment in homes to allow reuse of grey water can be expensive and may not be affordable to those on lower income.
Water management to prepare for and prevent flooding can support mobility by reducing potential disruption to transport and travel routes.
Water management to prepare for and prevent flooding can help to protect housing from water damage.
Sustainable urban drainage systems (SUDS) involving vegetation can act as carbon capture and storage solutions.
Blue' space infrastructure (e.g. in parks, wetlands) can help to regulate the temperature during heat waves.
Harvesting rainwater can prevent excessive run-off, reducing soil erosion and nutrient loss.
Sustainable water management practices can create healthy river corridors that are better able to house biodiversity.
Planting marsh and trees as flood protection measures may help cleanse the air.

Sustainable urban drainage systems (SUDS) can reduce the runoff of excessive fertilizer use. Proper treatment of grey water sources that contain nitrogen and phosphorus due to excessive fertilizer use will reduce the harms caused by releasing this water into the land (e.g. through algal blooms).
Sustainable urban drainage systems (SUDS) create permeable surfaces to reduce chemical pollution via run-off.
Freshwater withdrawals can be reduced by making efficient use of untreated (grey) water.
cycle_water.description: Glasgow recognises the value of clean water. It maximises opportunities for grey water recycling, rainwater harvesting, and manages wastewater sustainably. The rivers are free from pollution and support healthy biodiversity.
cycle_water.target: Glasgow efficiently uses untreated water for growing, gardening, washing, and cleaning, and employs green infrastructure, nature-based solutions, and sustainable urban drainage systems. It embraces urban design practices that promote adaptation through rain gardens, flood plains, more permeable surfaces, and healthy river corridors that provide wildlife habitat.

adjacent: Growth in local, renewable energy infrastructure can create sustainable jobs supporting income and work. However, some jobs may be lost in current energy industries before they are replaced in the green energy sector.
Increasing energy produced by renewable means will improve energy security and drive down energy prices.
Opportunities for community owned and managed clean energy production could improve social equity if the necessary support is in place for equitable access (e.g. training and capacity building).
Expensive green energy infrastructure may put pressure on other local budgets including culture.
New opportunities around renewable energy infrastructure could benefit women and girls, who are under-represented in engineering and technology disciplines, and improve equality and diversity.
Community-owned energy may help democratise the power sector and support local political voice and engagement.
Opportunities for community owned and managed clean energy production can bring members of the community together.

Growth in local, renewable energy infrastructure can create training opportunities, supporting education. However, expensive green energy infrastructure may put pressure on other local budgets, including education.
Renewable energy programs can support sustainable fresh water management and conservation.
Harvesting clean energy could reduce air pollution from the use of wood-burning stoves, and burning fossil fuels.
Harvesting clean energy could reduce air pollution from burning fossil fuels.
Replacing fossil fuel energy by harvesting clean energy will reduce CO2 emissions contributing to ocean acidification.
Replacing fossil fuel energy by harvesting clean energy will reduce CO2 emissions contributing to climate change.
Demand for materials and transition metals for new energy infrastructure may result in land conversion and have a damaging global material footprint.
Renewable energy programs can support sustainable fresh water management and conservation.
Demand for materials and transition metals for new energy infrastructure, and disposal of their waste products, may cause chemical pollution.
Better local energy security can support peace and justice by increasing Glasgow/Scotland’s political leverage and minimising its vulnerability to international conflicts.
Without transparent supply chains, work in the mining/extraction industry for materials required for renewable energy production may be dangerous or exploitative.

Global knowledge exchange could support communities elsewhere to benefit from harvesting energy, increasing global social equity. However, transparent supply chains and waste management processes for energy harvesting solutions are needed to preserve social equity.
harvest_energy.description: The Glasgow energy mix is harvested from renewable sources to benefit Glasgow residents and businesses. Glasgow pursues renewable energy generation and storage solutions.
harvest_energy.target: Glasgow maximises the use of solar, wind, water, and ground-source heat for its energy, distributed through local heat networks. It grants more approvals for solar power and low-carbon energy infrastructure on publicly owned buildings and ensures all new buildings are fitted with solar panels and zero-carbon heat sources. Glasgow explores new methods of generating and storing renewable energy, such as kinetic energy and 'Park Power' from parks and open spaces.

adjacent: Measures to regulate the temperature within Glasgow such as creating green and blue spaces, will minimise the risk of urban heat island effect during heat waves and its associated health harms e.g. stroke, overheating.
Green and blue spaces created to regulate the temperature can also be used for leisure and physical activity, which will enhance wellbeing.
Green and blue spaces created to regulate the temperature could help to house biodiversity.
Green and blue spaces created to regulate the temperature could help to store carbon.
Regulating the temperature and reducing the amount of atmospheric heat released from Glasgow will also reduce its contribution to climate change.
regulate_the_temperature.description: Considered design of the natural and built environment in Glasgow creates a balance of green, grey, and blue spaces that contribute to temperature regulation.
regulate_the_temperature.target: Glasgow focuses on creating more urban green spaces to achieve a better balance between 'urban' and 'natural' spaces. It maximises small spaces for plants and trees, such as pocket street parks.

adjacent: Keeping soils free from toxins supports good health, preventing diseases associated with inhaling dust and contaminants from polluted ground during dry periods.
Decontaminating vacant and derelict land may improve social equity, as the majority of sites are in deprived neighbourhoods.
Regeneration of vacant and derelict land could preserve heritage and culture through conserving Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSIs).
Decisions on new uses for vacant and derelict land could be directed by community voices.
Putting vacant and derelict land into productive use may have community and social benefits.
Soil quality impacts the abundance and nutritional quality of food, and restoring contaminated land could open opportunities for local growing initiatives and allotments.
Decontaminating vacant and derelict land sites may have beneficial psychological effects for people who live near them, enhancing wellbeing.
Improving soil quality makes it more effective at filtration, increasing its ability to cycle water, and reducing soil pollution reduces the risks of contaminating water systems with toxins.
build_&_protect_soil.description: Soil in Glasgow is healthy, nutrient-rich, and fertile, which supports healthy biodiversity, food growth, and diverse green spaces.
build_&_protect_soil.target: Glasgow minimises impermeable hard surfaces and encourages permeable surfaces. It provides spaces to support soil health through composting, regenerative agriculture, and hosting biodiversity. Glasgow also decontaminates and transforms vacant and derelict land sites to improve soil health and conserves Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSIs).

adjacent: Involvement in the upkeep and stewardship of green and blue spaces that enhance wellbeing may provide opportunities for income and work and volunteering.
Glasgow's open spaces can support mental and physical health when used for leisure and as 'green gyms’.
If Glasgow's parks are inclusive, accessible spaces they can support social equity.
If Glasgow's parks are inclusive, accessible spaces they can promote equality in diversity.
Glasgow's green spaces can support accessible and inclusive venues for cultural activities, for example, open air theatre.
The local community could have the opportunity to be involved in the upkeep and stewardship of green and blue spaces that enhance wellbeing.
Glasgow's green spaces can provide opportunities for local food growing initiatives.
Redesign of green and blue spaces for community benefits and to enhance wellbeing could also feature carbon capture and storage solutions.
Parks and other green and blue spaces designed to enhance wellbeing can also help to regulate the temperature.
enhance_wellbeing.description: Green and blue spaces across Glasgow are plentiful, pleasant, accessible to all, and clean.
enhance_wellbeing.target: Glasgow's open spaces serve multiple purposes, including leisure, community venues, and connecting with nature. The local community is engaged in the upkeep and stewardship of green and blue spaces, and support is provided to build capacity for volunteering. Glasgow prioritises the transformation of polluted, vacant, or derelict green and blue sites for the benefit of the community, and enacts the Glasgow Clyde Valley Green Network blueprint.

adjacent: Sustainably grown and responsibly sourced food is typically more expensive, and therefore potentially unaffordable within the income of many Glasgow citizens.
Moving to more sustainable plant-based food sources has been shown to have health benefits.
Changing to more globally responsible diets and food sources may reduce social equity if they are not equitably available to all Glaswegians.
Changing to more globally responsible food sources could improve the quality of Glaswegian's diets if they are affordable and accessible, but may other reduce choice and increase costs.
More sustainable food production local to Glasgow can support better water conservation.
More sustainable food production local to Glasgow can support better soil health and protection of soil nutrients.
Reducing livestock farming that causes large greenhouse gas emissions will reduce climate change.
Less intensive farming methods and more plant-based rather than livestock farming requires less land conversion.
Reducing fertilizer use in food growing, by promoting organic farming methods, will reduce nutrient runoff and associated harms.
Sustainable food production methods prioritise water conservation, reducing fresh water withdrawals.
Robust and sustainable food supplies can protect peace by reducing the displacement and conflict caused by famine.
Ensuring adequate and nutritious diets are available for global populations will improve health and reduce illness/deaths caused by malnutrition.
Changes to more sustainable food production methods will change the types of work available in this industry.
More responsible food imports to Glasgow will reduce pressure on food supplies for vulnerable global populations, improving equitable access to food worldwide.
More sustainable and less intensive methods of food production will reduce global energy usage.
More sustainable and less intensive methods of food production will reduce water consumption and increase water security for global populations.
food.description: Glasgow supports a human rights approach to food for all.
food.target: Glasgow does not import food for consumption here at the expense of more distant communities. Glaswegians do not consume unsustainable amounts of food that global populations rely on e.g. quinoa, nor foods that cause deforestation e.g. beef, avocadoes. Local and low-carbon food production is supported to ease pressure on the global agricultural system. Information is made easily available about healthy and sustainable diets e.g. methods and benefits of switching to primarily plant-based food.

adjacent: Responsible global water consumption may put certain industries based in Glasgow at risk, e.g. retail/consumption of fast fashion.
Responsible water consumption in Glasgow could reduce food insecurity due to threats of drought and famine globally.
water.description: Glasgow does not use more than its fair share of water, either directly or indirectly (through imported goods).
water.target: Glasgow does not deplete global water supplies by importing unsustainable amounts of products that use water intensively, such as fast fashion. Glasgow does not pollute the wider water systems e.g. through antibiotics, nutrients in salmon feed, or microplastics. Material goods and clothing are reused and recycled, to reduce industrial burdens on global water supplies. Decontamination of vacant and derelict land sites, and tighter regulation and enforcement of environmental standards, reduces pollution in waterways.

health.description: Glasgow acts to improve global health and wellbeing, and does not exacerbate existing threats to health and wellbeing through the working and industrial practices in its supply chains and recruitment practices.
health.target: Procurement practices are overhauled and supply chains coming into Glasgow do not involve dangerous or hazardous working conditions such as unsafe mining or child labour. Glasgow trains enough local citizens to fill essential health sector jobs, avoiding the tendency to recruit from other nations at levels that leave their local populations underserved. Food exported from Glasgow and its regions (such as fish) is free from harmful toxins e.g. heavy metals. The labels on products for sale in Glasgow are improved to offer trustworthy information about the conditions and wellbeing of workers in the supply chain.

adjacent: Improved education for all may offer more opportunities for women/girls, improving gender equality outcomes.
education.description: Glasgow supports and advocates for equal rights and access to education for all global populations.
education.target: Students worldwide are able to benefit from Glasgow's high-quality universities. Opportunities for global collaboration support gender and social equity (lower international fees, more ways to participate remotely) and sustainability (not dependent on high-carbon transport e.g. flying). Student exchange programmes are established and extended to build worldwide solidarity between students and share multidirectional learning. Goods in Glasgow's supply chains are not provided by child labour, which removes the opportunities for children worldwide to receive an education.

housing.description: Glasgow does not contribute to conditions that threaten the stability and security of places and materials for global communities.
housing.target: Glasgow reduces its contribution to climate change via CO2 emissions, which is causing floods, crop failures and rising sea levels in particularly vulnerable global communities e.g. The Island Nations. Direct and indirect Greenhouse Gas emissions in the most intensive sectors such as transport, agriculture, and heating, are minimized.

adjacent: Supporting global energy justice through renewable innovation could offer new sustainable work opportunities in Glasgow
Supporting global energy justice through renewable innovation could offer new education opportunities in Glasgow
energy.description: Glasgow uses and produces energy in ways that contribute to global Net Zero ambitions, and is considerate in its direct and indirect use of energy to minimise global energy consumption.
energy.target: Glasgow is developing methods of green energy generation and storage that can be exported and shared worldwide, to reduce other nations' dependence on extracting and burning fossil fuels. Glasgow's material footprint is minimized, to reduce embedded emissions, and is not supplied by goods or products that are made using fossil fuel energy.

income_&_work.description: Glasgow supports Fair Trade principles and good working conditions for all workers involved in its supply chains.
income_&_work.target: Glasgow does not import goods that are produced using forced labor, child labor, or hazardous working conditions. Initiatives are in place to minimize the need for new goods such as textiles that are likely products of poor working conditions e.g. setting up school uniform or sports uniform banks. Trade-offs are acknowledged and managed between Glasgow's immediate need for certain goods (such as personal technology) and the poorly regulated countries and industries that supply them (including dangerous mining and factories).

adjacent: Stopping investment in harmful practices and businesses that reduce social equity and fuel conflict can increase global peace and justice.
Stopping investment in harmful practices and businesses that reduce social equity will reduce exploitation in the global workforce.
social_equity.description: Glasgow takes responsibility as a Global North city to raise living standards worldwide, and reduce global inequalities.
social_equity.target: Glasgow develops world-leading sustainable procurement practices and reduces its consumption of products from exploitative industries that erode social equity. Glasgow makes progress towards climate neutrality without increasing the burden on other countries e.g. through exporting waste. Glasgow does not fund or invest in practices or businesses that cause social or ecological harm e.g. through pension funds. Glaswegians are able to access better information and choice in relation to the social footprint of the goods and services consumed in the city.

equality_in_diversity.description: Glasgow is welcoming to all people from all cultures and delivers healthy cultural inclusion. Glasgow's activities do not support or uphold regimes with poor human rights records.
equality_in_diversity.target: We challenge threats to equality, such as 'hostile environment' policies.

community_&_networks.description: Glaswegians act as 'global citizens' to build community and solidarity worldwide.
community_&_networks.target: Cultural and educational exchange programmes build strong networks and connection between Glasgow residents and global populations. Glasgow supports and welcomes climate refugees, and provides training and employment opportunities for newcomers to the city.

political_voice.description: Glasgow sets a leading example of free, inclusive and intergenerationally just democratic engagement in political decisions.
political_voice.target: n/a - no further suggestions made in workshops

peace_&_justice.description: Glasgow ensures representation, inclusion, and protection of the rights of those most vulnerable to the effects of climate change.
peace_&_justice.target: Glasgow's climate and ecological footprints are minimized, lessening its contribution to global instability, forced migration, and conflicts. Clean local energy reduces Glasgow's dependence on imported fossil fuels e.g. gas. Short-term and long-term gains are carefully balanced e.g. Glaswegians who can afford to, are making certain sacrifices locally, to secure the long-term futures of people globally. Transparency and comprehensive reporting is insisted upon, from corporations and SMEs, about the footprint of their products and services. Glasgow supports the work of existing refugee organisations e.g. Refuweegee.

adjacent: Food waste/biomass could be used for local clean energy production.
People's food choices have a huge impact on health, with nutritious, balanced diets helping to prevent diseases such as diabetes, stroke, and heart disease.
Initiatives such as local food growing, shared allotments, and community kitchens/pantries can bring people together and strengthen community ties.
Making healthy and sustainable food options affordable will support social equity by ensuring equal access opportunities.
Local food growing such as allotments can help increase biodiversity.
More sustainable and diverse diets can help protect biodiversity (e.g. by not overfishing, preventing deforestation).
Eating diets that cause lower carbon emissions (e.g. more plant-based diets) can help reduce climate change.
Food production for plant-based diets is less intensive in terms of land usage, helping to prevent land conversion.
Food production for plant-based diets uses less water than meat production, helping to prevent freshwater withdrawals.
Changes to diets need to be properly understood to avoid undermining food security elsewhere through unsustainable food choices (e.g. avocados, quinoa are not sustainable food sources).
Glasgow's food imports need to consider the conditions (income and work) of people working in the global supply chains.
food.description: Everyone in Glasgow has affordable access to nourishing and sustainable food. There is no food poverty, and no need for food banks.
food.target: Local community food growing and food sharing initiatives are widespread, and healthy food options are more accessible and affordable than ultra-processed options.

adjacent: Widespread, near-constant use of the internet and processing of data uses a lot of energy.
Universal access to fast, affordable internet may offer fairer access to employment (income and work) opportunities.
Universal access to fast, affordable internet may offer fairer access to education opportunities.
connectivity.description: All citizens in Glasgow have access to fast, affordable broadband and are supported in accessing online communication networks and the internet. There are no digital inequalities by age, wealth, or education status.
connectivity.target: n/a - no further suggestions made in workshops

adjacent: Creating more affordable new housing will increase the amount of income people have available to spend on other things.
Higher quality and warm housing supports good health.
Community networks can be improved if housing is built where it is most needed.
Well-insulated, energy efficient housing will minimise domestic energy use for heating.
To encourage active travel housing could be adapted to include improved storage for bikes and other active travel equipment.
New housing developments could include solar panels to harvest energy.
Construction of new housing developments should be planned to minimise the amount of pollutants being released into the air.
New housing developments could lead to the loss of green space, and the wellbeing benefits these spaces bring.
Plans for new housing sites need to consider how they can support urban spaces to cycle water.
New housing developments should be designed to support biodiversity net gain. There is a risk of loss of biodiversity if housing sites are built on biodiverse land.
There is a risk of loss of biodiversity if housing sites are built on biodiverse land.
Construction of new housing developments should be planned to minimise the amount of pollutants being released into the air.

Reducing or replacing fossil-fuel powered heating in homes will reduce the ocean acidification caused by greenhouse gas emissions. However, the construction sector is a large contributor to these emissions, which must be accounted for when planning new build/retrofitting housing.

Reducing or replacing fossil-fuel powered heating in homes will reduce the climate change caused by greenhouse gas emissions. However, the construction sector is a large contributor to these emissions, which must be accounted for when planning new build/retrofitting housing.
New housing developments risk unsustainable land conversion.
Targeted retrofit of the houses that need this most could increase social equity.
housing.description: Homes for all residents, in all tenures, are affordable, secure, energy-efficient, and free from health hazards.
housing.target: Glasgow celebrates its architectural heritage and modernizes/retrofits tenements, builds and regenerates beautiful, low-carbon social housing, and prioritizes residents' interests over landlords' profits. It supports national-level housing reform and provides additional co-benefits to communities through housing services and social landlords.

adjacent: Adequate water reserves support nature, allowing plants to grow which then store carbon.
Being more careful with water usage will improve water resilience, lessening the impact on freshwater withdrawal.
Responsible re-use of grey water in gardens or agriculture can reduce the risk of chemical pollution from reused water sources.
Preventing over use of fresh water locally is part of global human rights approach to water, by not using more than our fair share.
water.description: Everyone's water requirements are met - clean, treated water for drinking, cooking, and hygiene is readily available.
water.target: Water resilience is improved by not over-using clean, treated water for growing, gardening, washing, cleaning, etc.

adjacent: A strong sense of community and belonging can combat loneliness and is good for health and wellbeing.
Communities that ‘cogovern’ spaces and services for mutual benefit may also have an enhanced democratic and political voice.
community.description: Glasgow is a friendly and welcoming city. All Glaswegians have opportunities to take an active role in their communities, supporting vital community connection and services.
community.target: There are widespread community sharing initiatives and communal resources, and more people have the ability to take part in volunteering. Plenty of community spaces are available for use in all seasons, and opportunities for local communities to act as stewards of these spaces.

adjacent: Healthier Glaswegians will be better equipped to take up income and work opportunities.
Smaller inequalities in health will improve social equity
Having good physical health is an enabling factor for taking up active travel, thereby increasing mobility.
Having good physical health is an enabling factor for involvement in community activities and networks.
health.description: All Glasgow citizens live long and healthy lives, and health inequalities are small. Glasgow's environment promotes physical health, enhances wellbeing, and supports good mental health.
health.target: Everyone lives in a health-promoting environment without contaminated soil and polluted land posing a health threat. High-quality green spaces, clean air, active travel routes, and plentiful cycle storage allow for physical activity. Glasgow eliminates disproportionate levels of excess deaths from substance abuse or suicide.

adjacent: Cultural industries can support long-term job creation in rewarding and socially valuable sectors, supporting income and work.
Cultural activities are important for wellbeing and can support good mental health.
Cultural events can promote equality in diversity and inclusion, using creative and innovative methods to amplify marginalised voices.
Artists and cultural practitioners can take an active creative role in involving local citizens in the process of sustainable transition and enhancing citizens’ political voice.

Artists and cultural practitioners can take an active creative role in community engagement, outreach, and participation, building solidarity and involving local citizens in the process of sustainable transition.
Artists and cultural practitioners can support the education system in developing culturally engaged and socially responsible young people.

The cultural sector may be able to leverage its influence to decarbonise the industry or change the ways cultural consumers travel to events, boosting methods of greener transport and sustainable mobility.

Cultural events and attractions that bring many visitors to the city may contribute to impacts such as air pollution, but the cultural sector may be able to leverage its influence to decarbonise the industry or change the ways cultural consumers travel to events.

Cultural events and attractions that bring many visitors to the city may contribute to impacts such as climate change, but the cultural sector may be able to leverage its influence to decarbonise the industry or change the ways cultural consumers travel to events.
culture.description: People in Glasgow enjoy a healthy 'work-life' balance with lots of opportunity for cultural, leisure, and wellbeing-promoting activities that are both affordable and inclusive.
culture.target: Our cultural assets such as museums and creative spaces contribute to wider city ambitions, such as job creation.

adjacent: A well-planned and well-resourced education sector can support income and work through a sustainable pipeline into decent employment.
Decent universal education can create shared opportunities and reduce social inequalities.
Education can be powerful tool for reducing economic and gender inequalities.
Schools meals can be used to provide and teach children about nutritious and low-carbon food.
School buildings can be good locations for solar panels to harvest energy.

Education and outdoor learning can create local, engaged citizens who are involved in projects and activities that benefit the local environment e.g. rewilding, tree-planting, leading to greater biodiversity.
Developing global networks and opening up universities to global students can provide educational opportunities for students worldwide.
education.description: A well-funded education system (schools, colleges, universities) gives equal access to all Glaswegians the foundation for life-long opportunity and fulfillment. Everyone in Glasgow is supported to realize their potential.
education.target: All children attend school without the additional challenges of poverty, such as hunger. Education providers emphasize the value of biodiversity and a healthy ecosystem for human prosperity, and support healthy meals, low-carbon travel, and physical activity.

adjacent: Sufficient income allows citizens to afford essential goods and services such energy.
Decent work and sufficient income is essential for good health and wellbeing.
Accessible, inclusive work opportunities can support social equity.
Sustainable job growth in the culture industry can benefit both work and the environment.
Accessible, inclusive work opportunities can support equality in diversity.
Sufficient income allows citizens to afford essential goods and services such water.
Sufficient income allows citizens to afford essential goods and services such food.
Sufficient income allows citizens to afford essential goods and services such housing.
Alternative business models such as social enterprises and cooperatives may foster a sense of community.
A move away from work in consumption-based industries towards more sustainable industries will reduce emissions that cause air pollution.
A move away from work in consumption-based industries towards more sustainable industries will reduce green house gases emissions that cause ocean acidification.
A move away from work in consumption-based industries towards more sustainable industries will reduce green house gases emissions that cause climate change.
A move away from work in consumption-based industries towards more sustainable or circular industries will reduce land conversion to extract raw materials.
A move away from work in consumption-based industries towards more sustainable or circular industries will reduce chemical pollution.
Glasgow industries can influence the working conditions of people worldwide by choosing responsible global supply chains.
income_&_work.description: All Glaswegians have sufficient income from a sustainable/fulfilling source. There is zero poverty in the city.
income_&_work.target: Job growth areas are in sustainable industries such as renewable energy, culture, and wellbeing services. Long-term investment is made in the skills and training to support these good quality jobs. Glasgow invests in and supports alternative business models such as social enterprises and cooperatives. Glasgow residents are connected to high-quality employment opportunities through accessible transport options and inclusive recruitment practices.

adjacent: Creating renewable energy infrastructure locally may support income and work through sustainable job creation.
Affordable energy for all Glaswegians will reduce fuel poverty and the health harms that come from living in cold and damp homes (e.g. respiratory conditions).
Affordable energy for all Glaswegians will reduce fuel poverty and improve social equity.
The energy sector could provide opportunities to support equality in diversity, for example by recruiting more women and girls who are typically underrepresented in this sector.
Community owned and managed renewable energy projects may benefit political voice as citizens increase their democratic oversight and engagement.
Locally managed renewable energy project can engage communities and bring them together.
Creating renewable energy infrastructure locally may provide valuable education and training for the green energy sector.
Decarbonisation of the energy sector will reduce air pollution associated with burning fossil fuels.
Decarbonisation of the energy sector will reduce greenhouse gas emissions and help to reduce ocean acidification.
Decarbonisation of the energy sector will reduce greenhouse gas emissions and help to reduce climate change.
Demand for materials for development of renewable energy infrastructure (e.g. batteries) may increase chemical pollution.
More locally (or nationally) owned energy reduces dependence on external energy sources (e.g. from authoritarian regimes) supporting global peace and justice.
Demand for materials for development of renewable energy infrastructure could create global income and work, but there is a risk of these being unsafe or exploitative roles.
energy.description: All of Glasgow's energy needs are met from renewable sources. Everyone is able to afford their energy requirements.
energy.target: Glasgow significantly reduces its energy consumption overall, particularly by combining energy efficiency measures with decarbonizing heating and reducing the consumption of high-consumption industries and individuals. It promotes more locally owned and managed renewable energy infrastructure within Glasgow and surrounding communities to generate community wealth.

adjacent: Increased social equity may lead to improved and fairer outcomes for income and work.
Increased social equity may lead to improved and fairer outcomes for health.
Increased social equity may lead to improved and fairer outcomes for education.
Increased social equity may result in better levels of democratic engagement and political voice.
Increased social equity may result in a better sense of community.
Inequality is known to drive and exacerbate climate change. Reversing this negative feedback loop could lead to mutual benefit for both social equity and climate outcomes.
social_equity.description: All Glasgow citizens are valued equally, and all Glasgow's communities benefit from inclusive access to, and representation in, city spaces and institutions.
social_equity.target: Dramatic improvement and investment in the fabric of historically poorer areas, improving access to and ownership of 'The Commons' across all communities. Glaswegians act as stewards of public resources for the benefit of future generations. VDL sites in deprived areas are regenerated to provide amenities (natural, cultural, social, economic) to those who most need them. Policy levers are employed to protect against gentrification. Patterns of intergenerational poverty are broken.

adjacent: Better connected networks and neighbourhoods through active travel routes and green public transport can provide access to more work opportunities. Costs of walking or running bikes and scooters (e.g. maintenance, insurance) are lower than running private cars, which may benefit income.

Active travel can be beneficial for physical and mental health, and reduced traffic levels could reduce road traffic accidents. Improved mobility and transport options can improve access to health care services.
Reducing social, physical, cultural and monetary barriers to activities such as cycling will positively impact social equity.
Reducing social, physical, cultural and monetary barriers to activities such as cycling will positively impact equality in diversity.
Better connected networks and neighbourhoods through active travel routes and green public transport can strengthen community ties.

Better connected networks and neighbourhoods through active travel routes and green public transport can provide access to more education opportunities. Travelling to school via active methods can improve children's readiness to learn.
Travel infrastructure designed with safety and inclusivity in mind e.g. well-lit paths, could lead to reduced crime, supporting peace and justice.
Better connected networks and neighbourhoods through active travel routes can provide more local opportunities to access goods such as nutritious food, and increase the demand for local food outlets.
There is the potential to harvest kinetic energy from active travel.
Reducing carbonised transport methods will reduce emissions and improve air quality.
Biodiversity could be increased by designing new and regenerated travel routes to support wildlife, for example, greening tram tracks or adding hedgerows along cycling or walking paths.
Greener transport methods and increased active travel can reduce global air pollution through a reduction in transport and car manufacturing emissions.
Greener transport methods and increased active travel can reduce climate change through a reduction in transport and car manufacturing emissions.
The demand for new materials to support the transition to electric transport may cause land conversion globally.

The transition to electric transport may increase chemical pollution from the increased use and poor disposal of batteries. Increased active travel over car use may reduce the demand for batteries and heavy metals that could cause chemical pollution.
The demand for materials to support the transition to electric transport may cause health harm through working conditions in industries such as mining.
The demand for materials to support the transition to electric transport may cause harm through poor working conditions in industries such as mining.
mobility.description: It is easy, safe, and affordable for Glaswegians and commuters to get around the city sustainably at all times of the day.
mobility.target: Glasgow's compact, liveable neighborhoods with access to key infrastructure and services are connected by a cheap, decarbonized, fully integrated public transport system that provides a regular service throughout the day and night. Glasgow is well connected to other cities and rural areas.

adjacent: If all voices in society are properly heard and equally represented this may benefit political voice.
If all voices in society are properly heard and equally represented this may benefit community kinship.
equality_in_diversity.description: Glasgow recognizes and celebrates the diversity of its communities. All Glaswegians, regardless of background or culture, have equal opportunities and access to everything Glasgow has to offer.
equality_in_diversity.target: The diversity of all Glasgow's neighborhoods is celebrated and reflected in decision-making and services, through different languages. Services and city spaces are used equally by all groups in society - ethnic diversity and gender equality - reflected, for example, in patterns of active travel.

adjacent: Use of citizens' assemblies can encourage more community engagement.
Inclusive processes of democracy could support equality in diversity.
political_voice.description: Glasgow takes an inclusive and proactive approach to policy and decision-making.
political_voice.target: Our political processes are informed by more inclusive citizen participation and engagement, valuing all voices, including quiet ones (of different ages and backgrounds too). Public spaces and tools such as citizens' assemblies are used to encourage more community engagement, and our political leaders demonstrate that they can be trusted.

adjacent: A safer city with reduced violent crime may make women and girls or other marginalised groups feel more confident to participate activities, increasing equality in diversity.
A fair justice system that citizens have faith in is good for democracy and supports political voice.
A fair justice system that citizens have faith in is good for community.
Reduced crime rates may make it feel safer to use active travel.
peace_&_justice.description: Glasgow prioritizes and resources residents' safety, peace, and protection.
peace_&_justice.target: Neighborhoods are safe and peaceful in all parts of the city, all individuals feel protected, and trust that resources are available to keep them safe, e.g., in parks and green spaces.
